Triggers.value: Being in a situation where someone has power over me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
constantly scan environment for signs of threat
make sure to stay close to exit

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, 'the person who harmed me' implies an identifiable individual perpetrator relationship, which is hard to reconcile with the otherwise impersonal trigger profile (sirens, smoke) and is clinically less coherent than cues linked to attack scenes or public danger. The other strategy items are severe but not contradictory, and the strong Triggers↔Maladaptive Strategies link is otherwise plausible.

issues.item: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts
issues.explanation: Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, 'Positive Reframing' implies a cognitive coping effort to dampen distress, whereas 'Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened' describes approaching the trauma site rather than avoiding it; this is internally inconsistent because the item label and content pull in opposite behavioral directions.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: This item is clinically discordant with the rest of the profile. The formulation only strongly links Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies, and the listed triggers are external terrorism-related cues (sirens, smoke, power imbalance) that plausibly connect to avoidance and checking. Self-harm to stop thinking about the event introduces a severe emotion-regulation/dissociation strategy that is not supported by any other selected items in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and is hard to reconcile as part of the same narrow trigger-driven loop described by the formulation. The rest of the maladaptive strategies are coherent; this item is the one that appears out of pattern.

vignette: Dr. Leela Patel, an 80-year-old South Asian woman who is divorced and formerly a dentist, has been grappling with the lasting impact of a terrorist attack she witnessed several years ago. The traumatic event left her feeling deeply vulnerable and fearful, particularly when she encounters specific triggers such as sirens, the smell of smoke, or situations where she feels a power imbalance. On the day of the incident, Leela was at her dental clinic in downtown Chicago when a group of terrorists attacked the city's financial district. The piercing wail of sirens echoed through the streets as emergency vehicles rushed to the scene. The overwhelming scent of smoke filled the air, and the chaos around her created an intense sense of powerlessness. This traumatic event has left indelible marks on Leela's psyche. Since then, everyday life has become a series of avoidances and constant vigilance. Sirens have become particularly triggering for her; every time she hears them, it instantly transports her back to that terrifying day. To manage this fear, she has adopted several maladaptive strategies that have gradually taken over her daily routine. She avoids going near the areas where she heard those sirens the most, even if it means taking a longer route home or skipping social gatherings. One of Leela's primary coping mechanisms is constantly scanning her environment for signs of threat. This hyper-vigilance has become so ingrained that she feels uncomfortable unless she can see all possible exits from any place she enters. She avoids crowded places and always positions herself near an exit when she must go out, which has made it increasingly difficult for her to maintain social connections. For instance, Leela used to enjoy attending professional conferences at the downtown hotel where she heard those sirens the day of the attack. Now, even just the thought of going there triggers intense anxiety. She has stopped attending these events altogether and finds herself isolating more often, which only exacerbates her fears. Moreover, the smell of smoke, reminiscent of that fateful day, also serves as a potent trigger for Leela. Even mild odors can evoke a sense of dread and panic. This fear has led her to avoid situations where she might encounter such smells, further limiting her ability to engage in normal activities. She avoids places like restaurants or public parks during times when barbecues are common. Her avoidance behaviors have created a vicious cycle that reinforces her triggers. The more she avoids certain locations and scents, the stronger those triggers become. Leela has come to believe that staying vigilant and avoiding potential threats is the only way to keep herself safe. This constant state of hyper-awareness and avoidance has taken a toll on her professional life as well. Her practice has seen a decline in patients due to her reluctance to work in certain areas or deal with potentially triggering situations. What frightens Leela most is that she cannot control these fears anymore. The triggers have become so pervasive that they color every aspect of her daily existence, making it nearly impossible for her to live without feeling on edge. She has come to the realization that her maladaptive strategies are no longer sustainable and are instead worsening her condition. Leela finally decided to seek help when she realized that these fears were not only limiting her life but also preventing her from connecting with family and friends in meaningful ways. Her primary hope is to regain some semblance of normalcy and to be able to engage in activities without being constantly haunted by the memories of that day. She hopes therapy will provide her with tools to manage her triggers and break the cycle of avoidance, allowing her to live a fuller life once again.
